description: We aim to build a web-based platform using harmonized MODIS and VIIRS fire data to visualize burning activity, analyze historical patterns, and detect unusual fire periods. The platform will provide interactive maps and calendars to support researchers, emergency responders, and land managers with clear, data-driven fire insights.
summary:
In 2012, global satellite fire detections appeared to quadruple overnight. Nothing burned four times harder; NASA’s Earth constellation simply transitioned from MODIS (1 km) to sharper VIIRS (375 m) sensors. Because a single flame registers as multiple fragmented VIIRS pixels, raw records create an artificial +270% spike that distorts two decades of climate baselines.

To resolve this, Team ASL NOVA developed EmberSync, an autonomous three-stage harmonization engine and interactive Burning Activity Calendar. Using cosine-latitude spatio-temporal clustering and an evolutionary multi-objective genetic algorithm, EmberSync discovers biome-adaptive clustering scales (0.80 km in rainforests to 1.50 km in savannas) and performs distributional quantile mapping against 3,891 co-incident ground-truth fires. It consolidates 83,226 NASA FIRMS detections into 34,869 physical events eliminating 58.1% of artificial count inflation while strictly conserving radiative energy without double-counting.

EmberSync is critical because climate modeling and disaster response require an unbiased historical record. By repairing the 2012 sensor discontinuity, EmberSync delivers a continuous 26-year baseline coupled with a Z-score anomaly engine, alerting emergency responders when fire seasons surge beyond historical norms.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

EmberSync addresses the sensor discontinuity between MODIS (about 1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) to improve the temporal consistency of long-term satellite fire observations. It runs in three stages.

Stage 1: Boundary-Aware Spatio-Temporal Clustering.

  • It processes NASA FIRMS active fire data and applies cosine-latitude, equal-ground-distance normalization so clustering radii stay physically consistent across latitudes.
  • Detections within the same 12-hour window are merged across cell boundaries using a vectorized Haversine-based Disjoint Set Union (DSU) algorithm.
  • In the global benchmark, 83,226 raw detections were consolidated into 34,869 estimated physical fire events, a 58.1% reduction.
  • Sensor-specific energy values are kept in separate channels to avoid duplicating energy.

Stage 2: Multi-Objective Evolutionary Genetic Algorithm.

  • EmberSync identifies 3,891 coincident detections seen by both satellites and uses them as an internal cross-sensor supervision signal.
  • A Genetic Algorithm (30 generations) optimizes a five-parameter chromosome C = [w_frp, p, w_bright, c_scale, R].
  • It jointly optimizes event-count parity and distributional energy parity, using log-space Quantile Mapping across the 10th to 90th percentiles.
  • The optimized radius feeds back into Stage 1, so the full dataset is reprocessed in a closed loop.

Stage 3: Burning Activity Calendar and Anomaly Detection.

  • Harmonized fire events are aggregated daily by biome.
  • A Day-of-Year rolling climatological baseline captures historical seasonal burning patterns.
  • A Z-score engine classifies each day as Normal (Z < 1.0), Elevated Risk (1.0 ≤ Z < 2.0), or Critical Anomaly (Z ≥ 2.0).
  • Results appear in an interactive 365-day calendar for monitoring seasonal variation and unusual fire activity.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Corrects the 2012 sensor discontinuity. It reduces the apparent rise in fire counts caused by the transition to higher-resolution VIIRS, improving comparability of long-term records.
  • Biome-adaptive spatial precision. Evolved, biome-dependent radii replace fixed global distances: 0.80 km for dense rainforest and 1.50 km for open savanna.
  • Sensor-specific energy preservation. Separate FRP channels prevent double-counting energy. In the Amazon Basin, the VIIRS distribution fell within 3% of the MODIS reference median.
  • Self-supervised calibration. Coincident MODIS/VIIRS observations serve as internal supervision, reducing reliance on external ground fire reports.
  • Accessible visualization. It is a lightweight browser app with no installation or build step. Before/After timeline comparisons and calendar heatmaps let researchers and operational users explore the results.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • More reliable climate modeling. It reduces the risk of mistaking a change in sensor resolution for a real increase in fire activity, giving a more consistent dataset for long-term trend analysis.
  • Better disaster risk assessment. Automated anomaly classes highlight deviations from seasonal norms, helping firefighters, forest rangers, and emergency agencies prioritize areas for investigation.
  • Ecosystem and biodiversity conservation. Biome-specific analysis across regions such as the Amazon Basin and Indo-Gangetic plains can help separate unusual burning from expected seasonal agricultural burning.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Data: NASA FIRMS, MODIS Collection 6.1 NRT (MCD14DL), VIIRS Suomi NPP 375 m NRT (VNP14IMGTDL).
  • Backend and science: Python 3, NumPy (vectorized computation), Pandas, and standard libraries (math, json, argparse).
  • Frontend: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3, Leaflet.js (maps with zoom-aware marker thinning), Chart.js (timelines and GA convergence curves).
  • Deployment: Git, GitHub, GitHub Pages, Linux Bash.
  • AI-assisted development: A custom multi-objective Genetic Algorithm was implemented for optimization. Perplexity AI supported literature discovery, Fable supported architectural cross-checking, Claude Code assisted with web app scaffolding, and Gemini supported scriptwriting and judging-criteria review.
  • Hardware: Standard consumer-grade Linux workstations with no GPU or cloud needed. Vectorized NumPy and DSU path compression process 83,000+ records in under 30 seconds.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Data-driven clustering. Evolutionary optimization finds biome-dependent parameters instead of a fixed global radius, with about a 1.9-fold difference between rainforest and savanna.
  • Closed-loop multi-objective optimization. Count parity and energy calibration are optimized together, and the evolved radius is fed back to reprocess the whole dataset.
  • Distributional harmonization. Because observation times, scan angles, and sensor traits make point-to-point FRP prediction unreliable, EmberSync aligns energy distributions with log-space Quantile Mapping.
  • Interactive Before/After timeline. A slider makes the effect of harmonization, especially around 2012, easy to see.
  • Harmonization plus anomaly detection. It goes beyond retrospective correction by combining seasonal baselines and automated anomaly classification in one monitoring application.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Geographic distance distortion: Cosine-latitude scaling keeps physical clustering distances consistent from the equator to high latitudes.
  • Diurnal patterns: 12-hour windows and day/night flags keep observations from different temporal phases separate.
  • Orbital geometry and sensor traits: We accounted for viewing geometry, resolution differences, and the MODIS scan-edge bowtie effect (Li et al., 2018).
  • Avoiding energy duplication: FRP from multiple satellites viewing the same fire is never summed as independent energy.
  • Scientific transparency: We clearly separate directly measured telemetry (the eight-day global benchmark) from the modeled 2000-2026 historical baseline, so modeled estimates are never presented as observations.
